text: Heads up: today's deploy is pushed to tomorrow. I'll post the new window here as soon as it's locked.

fix(auth): guard null user in login handler

The login handler dereferenced the user record returned by the session
lookup without checking it. When the lookup returned null (unknown email,
expired or revoked token) the request crashed with a null pointer instead
of failing the login.

Return 401 when the lookup yields no user. Added a regression test for the
unknown-email path.

## Add rate limiting to the API

### What
Adds per-client rate limiting to all public API routes. Requests over the limit get `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header.

### Why
A single misbehaving client can currently saturate the request pool and degrade the API for everyone. Rate limiting caps the blast radius and gives us a lever we can tune per route without a deploy.

### How
- Sliding-window counter in Redis, keyed by API key when present, falling back to client IP.
- Default limit: 100 requests / 60s per key. Overridable per route.
- Middleware runs before auth-heavy work so rejected requests cost near-nothing.
- Response headers on every request: `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`. On rejection: `Retry-After` in seconds.
- Limits are read from config at request time, so they can be changed without a redeploy.

### Behavior notes
- **Fail-open.** If Redis is unavailable the middleware allows the request and logs an error. Availability over enforcement; flip the `RATE_LIMIT_FAIL_CLOSED` flag if that's the wrong trade for your environment.
- **IP fallback is coarse.** Unauthenticated clients behind shared NAT share a bucket. Acceptable for now; authenticated traffic is keyed correctly.
- Internal service-to-service tokens are exempt via allowlist.

### Config
| Var | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RATE_LIMIT_REQUESTS` | 100 | Requests per window |
| `RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SEC` | 60 | Window length |
| `RATE_LIMIT_FAIL_CLOSED` | false | Reject when Redis is down |

### Testing
- Unit tests for the window counter, including boundary rollover.
- Integration test: 101st request in a window returns 429 with `Retry-After`.
- Load test at 2x expected peak: p99 middleware overhead 1.2ms.

### Rollout
1. Ship with limits set high enough to reject nothing (`RATE_LIMIT_REQUESTS=100000`).
2. Watch the `rate_limit.would_reject` metric for one week to size real limits.
3. Lower to the real value.

Rollback is a config change, not a revert.

**→ Get `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the slow query now and compare it to the plan it used to have — a query that degrades overnight almost always means the planner switched strategies, not that the query got harder.**

**→ Check statistics first — the most common cause.** `SELECT relname, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'your_table';` If `last_analyze` is old or a bulk load landed since, run `ANALYZE your_table;` and re-time. Stale stats make the planner pick a seq scan or a nested loop that was right at 10k rows and catastrophic at 10M.

**→ Check bloat and dead tuples.** High `n_dead_tup` relative to `n_live_tup` means autovacuum is falling behind and scans read pages that hold nothing. `VACUUM (ANALYZE)` and re-time.

**→ Check whether the index is still being used.** In the plan, look for a seq scan where you expect an index scan. `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` tells you if the index is being hit at all. An index goes unused when its stats are stale, when the query got a new predicate, or when a data-type mismatch defeats it.

**→ Look at rows estimated vs rows actual in the plan.** That gap is the diagnosis. Estimate 100, actual 2,000,000 means the planner chose based on a lie — fix the stats or raise `default_statistics_target` on the offending column, don't rewrite the query yet.

**→ Rule out that it isn't the query.** Check `pg_stat_activity` for `wait_event_type = 'Lock'` and `pg_locks` for blockers; check host CPU, IO wait, and whether the working set stopped fitting in `shared_buffers`. A query "getting slow" is sometimes a neighbor eating the cache.

**→ Check what changed last week, in this order:** data volume, a new index or a dropped one, a schema or type change, a Postgres minor-version upgrade, a connection-pooler or config change. The timeline is evidence.

**→ Reproduce before you tune.** Run it on a copy with production stats. Fixes applied against a plan you can't reproduce are guesses, and `ANALYZE` on a live table can change the plan under you mid-investigation.

**→ Risk:** don't add an index as the first move. It hides a stats problem, costs write throughput permanently, and you'll never find the real cause.

**→ REST. Small team, mobile backend — GraphQL's payoff needs client diversity and schema-ownership discipline you don't have yet.**

**→ What GraphQL actually buys you:** one round trip for a screen that needs data from four resources, and clients that change their data needs without a backend deploy. Both matter most when you have many client types or a slow release train.

**→ What it costs:** N+1 resolution needs DataLoader-style batching or your database melts; caching moves from free (HTTP/CDN on GET) to something you build; query cost limiting and depth limiting are mandatory on a public endpoint or you've shipped a DoS vector; error handling is 200-with-errors, which breaks naive client code. That's a standing tax on a small team.

**→ Mobile's real constraints are round trips and payload size.** REST handles both without GraphQL: give each screen a purpose-built endpoint (`GET /home-feed` returning exactly what that screen renders), plus `?fields=` or sparse responses where payload matters. This is 90% of GraphQL's benefit for 10% of the machinery.

**→ Pick GraphQL only if you hit two or more of these:** three-plus distinct clients with different data needs, App Store review latency making backend-driven data shape genuinely valuable, a federation story across multiple services, or a client team that's blocked on backend endpoint changes weekly.

**→ Old app versions never die.** Whatever you choose, version your responses and never remove a field a shipped client reads. This bites REST and GraphQL equally, and it's the constraint people forget until a 2-year-old install crashes.

**→ The cheap hedge:** build REST now, and if the screen-assembly pain shows up, add a thin GraphQL or BFF layer in front of the same services. Going REST → GraphQL later is normal. Going GraphQL → REST after you've built resolvers is a rewrite.

**→ An index is a separate sorted data structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations, so the database can jump to matching rows instead of reading the whole table — and it hurts when writes outnumber the reads it accelerates, or when it's too unselective to skip much work.**

**→ Mechanically:** without an index, finding `WHERE email = 'x'` means a sequential scan — read every row. With one, the database binary-searches the sorted structure (log n) and follows the pointer. Millions of rows scanned becomes a handful of page reads.

**→ Indexes also serve ordering and grouping,** not just lookups. An index on `created_at` can satisfy `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20` with no sort step at all.

**→ Cost 1 — every write pays.** Each `INSERT`, `UPDATE` of an indexed column, and `DELETE` must update every index on the table. Ten indexes means ten extra structures maintained per write. On a write-heavy table this is the dominant cost, and it's invisible in read benchmarks.

**→ Cost 2 — storage and memory.** Indexes can rival the table in size. They compete with the table for cache; a big rarely-used index evicts pages you actually needed.

**→ Hurts when selectivity is low.** An index on a boolean, or a status column where 90% of rows are `'active'`, doesn't narrow anything. The planner correctly ignores it, and you paid the write cost for nothing. Rule of thumb: an index earns its place when a lookup returns under roughly 5-10% of the table.

**→ Hurts when it's redundant.** A composite index on `(a, b)` already serves queries filtering on `a` alone — leftmost-prefix. A separate index on `a` is pure overhead. This is the most common wasted index in real schemas.

**→ Hurts when the query can't use it.** `WHERE lower(email) = 'x'` skips a plain index on `email` (you need an expression index). Leading wildcards (`LIKE '%foo'`) skip it. Type mismatches skip it. The index exists, costs writes, and does nothing.

**→ Hurts by misleading the planner.** A bad or stale-statistics index can cause the planner to pick an index scan with random IO where a sequential scan would have been faster. More indexes means more plans to choose badly among.

**→ Bulk loads:** dropping indexes before a large import and rebuilding after is often dramatically faster than loading with them in place.

**→ How to decide, not guess:** read the query plan before and after; check whether the index is ever used (`pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0` means delete it). Build on a replica or with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` — a plain `CREATE INDEX` locks writes on the table for its duration.

**→ Worth it only if your pain is Jira's speed and complexity, not your own process — Linear is faster and better designed, but it will not fix a team that doesn't agree on how work is tracked.**

**→ What you actually gain:** a UI that responds in milliseconds instead of seconds, a data model with maybe a tenth of Jira's concepts, keyboard-driven navigation, cycles that auto-roll unfinished work, and a default setup that a new engineer understands in ten minutes. The daily friction difference is large and real.

**→ What you give up.** Jira's configurability is the point for some teams: arbitrary custom workflows with per-transition rules and validators, granular field-level permissions, deep Atlassian integration (Confluence, Bitbucket, Jira Service Management), Advanced Roadmaps for cross-team capacity planning, and a plugin marketplace with something for every niche. Linear deliberately doesn't do most of that.

**→ Weigh these, in order of how often they kill migrations:**

**→ 1. Who else uses your tracker.** If support, legal, marketing, or an external client files tickets in Jira, or if service desk / SLA workflows run there, you're not migrating — you're splitting into two tools. That's usually worse than staying.

**→ 2. Compliance and audit.** If you need SOC 2 / ISO evidence chains tying tickets to approvals, or regulated audit trails and field-level permissions, verify Linear's controls against your auditor's actual asks before anything else. This is the most common late-stage blocker.

**→ 3. History fidelity.** Linear's Jira importer moves issues, comments, and status. Expect losses on: custom fields with no Linear equivalent, worklogs and time tracking, attachments in some configurations, complex link types, and formatting in long descriptions. Decide now whether you need history to be queryable or just archived — keeping Jira read-only for a year is a legitimate answer and much cheaper than perfect migration.

**→ 4. Integrations you'd have to rebuild.** Inventory every automation touching Jira: CI status posting, release notes generation, Slack alerts, incident tooling, custom scripts against the Jira API. Each is migration work nobody budgets for.

**→ 5. Cost.** Compare at your real headcount on the tier you'd actually need, and include Jira's ecosystem — you may be paying for plugins you'd stop needing. Prices change; get current numbers from both vendors rather than trusting any figure you read.

**→ 6. Reporting your leadership already depends on.** If someone above you reads a specific Jira dashboard every week, find out whether Linear reproduces it before you commit. "We'll figure out reporting later" is how migrations get reversed.

**→ How to decide cheaply:** run one team on Linear for a full quarter with real work, keeping Jira live. Measure whether planning meetings shortened and whether people actually update tickets. If the trial team asks to go back, you have your answer for free.

**→ The honest failure mode:** teams migrate expecting a process fix, get a two-to-four-week disruption plus lost history, and land with the same unclear priorities in a prettier tool. If your complaint is "nobody knows what to work on," fix that first — the tool is downstream of it.

**→ Instrument the funnel into sub-steps first — "signup to first action" is too coarse to diagnose, and 60% is a range that hides at least three different failures.**

**→ Split the gap into observable events.** Signup submitted → account created → email verified (if required) → first login/session → onboarding screen reached → first action completed. Drop is almost never spread evenly; one of those edges is eating most of it. You can't fix what you can't localize.

**→ Segment every step by device, browser, OS, acquisition channel, geography, and account type.** A single broken combination (iOS Safari, one ad campaign sending mismatched-intent traffic, one locale) routinely masquerades as a broad funnel problem.

**→ Check the boring technical causes before behavioral ones:** verification emails landing in spam or delayed, a required field failing validation silently, OAuth callback breaking on one provider, slow first-load on mobile networks, an error state that renders as a blank screen. Pull server error rates and client-side JS errors for users in the gap specifically.

**→ Look at time-to-drop.** Users leaving in under 10 seconds means broken or misleading — page failed, or the product isn't what the ad promised. Users leaving after 2 minutes means confused or blocked — they tried and couldn't. Different fixes entirely.

**→ Watch session recordings for 20-30 dropped users.** Cheapest high-signal step available and it usually takes an afternoon. You'll see rage clicks, dead ends, and the exact field people abandon on. Do this before designing any experiment.

**→ Ask whether "first action" requires something they don't have yet:** data to import, teammates to invite, a payment method, an integration to connect, permissions from their IT. Empty-state dependency is the single most common cause of this exact drop shape. If the product is useless until they do setup work, the fix is sample data or a demo mode, not better copy.

**→ Email a sample of dropped users and ask.** 5 replies from real drop-offs beat a week of dashboard analysis. Offer nothing, ask one question: "What were you trying to do when you stopped?"

**→ Verify your tracking before trusting the number.** Ad blockers, missing events on some platforms, bot signups, and a "first action" definition that excludes things users legitimately do first will all inflate an apparent drop. Reconcile the analytics count against the database count for one day. Fixing an instrumentation artifact is embarrassing but cheap.

**→ Benchmark caveat:** 60% signup-to-activation is bad but not catastrophic for self-serve products. Don't burn a quarter chasing zero. Find the one segment or step that's far worse than the rest, fix that, remeasure.

**→ Be specific about the behavior and its impact, then shut up and let them respond — vagueness and monologue are what demoralize people, not criticism itself.**

**→ Do it privately, soon, and in person or on video.** Delayed feedback reads as ambush ("you've been thinking this for months?"). Written-only feedback strips tone and gets reread at 11pm in the worst possible voice.

**→ Lead with the actual point in the first 30 seconds.** "I want to talk about how the API review went" — not five minutes of warm-up. The warm-up doesn't soften anything; it just makes them brace while they decode what's coming.

**→ Name behavior, not character.** "The last three PRs went out without tests, and two of them broke staging" is actionable. "You're careless" is an identity attack they can only accept or fight. Never use "always" or "never" — one counterexample lets them dismiss the whole thing.

**→ State the impact concretely.** Who was affected, what it cost, why it matters. Impact is what converts "my manager's preference" into "a real problem." Without it, feedback sounds like taste.

**→ Then stop talking and ask.** "What's your read on it?" You may learn the cause is a blocker you created — unclear priorities, an impossible deadline, missing access. Skipping this is how managers confidently correct the wrong thing.

**→ Skip the compliment sandwich.** People discard the praise as padding and stop trusting your genuine praise later. Be direct, and be warm in your delivery — those aren't in tension.

**→ Separate feedback from evaluation, explicitly.** Say whether this is a course-correction or something affecting their rating. Ambiguity makes people assume the worst and spiral. If their job is not at risk, say so plainly; if it is, say that plainly too — never imply it and leave them guessing.

**→ Close with one specific change and a check-in date.** "For the next two weeks, tests in the PR before review, and let's look at it again on the 15th." One change, not five. Five means none.

**→ Ask what support they need,** and then actually provide it. Feedback without removed obstacles is just pressure.

**→ Write a short recap afterward** — what you discussed, what was agreed, when you'll revisit. Protects both of you, and prevents the meeting being remembered as harsher or softer than it was.

**→ The failure mode to avoid:** softening until the message doesn't land. They walk out relieved, nothing changes, and in six months you're having a much worse conversation about a pattern you never clearly flagged. Kindness that costs them their job later isn't kindness.

**→ 502 Bad Gateway: a server acting as a proxy or gateway got an invalid or empty response from the upstream server it was forwarding your request to.**

**→ The fault is upstream, not in your request.** Nothing about the request is malformed — retrying it unchanged can succeed.

**→ Common causes:** the upstream process crashed or isn't listening, the upstream took longer than the proxy's timeout, the proxy is pointed at a wrong host/port, or the response was malformed or too large for the proxy's buffers.

**→ Distinct from its neighbors.** 503 = the server is up but refusing (overloaded, maintenance). 504 = the upstream specifically timed out. 502 = the upstream answered with garbage, or didn't answer at all.

**→ Debug from the proxy's error log** (nginx, load balancer, CDN) — the proxy decided to return the 502, so it holds the reason. The app log may show nothing at all.

**→ A race condition is when two things run at overlapping times and the result depends on which one happens to get there first — so the same code gives different answers on different runs.**

**→ The single-threaded assumption that breaks:** you're used to line 2 finishing completely before line 3 starts, and to nothing else touching your variables in between. With concurrency, both of those stop being true.

**→ The canonical example.** Two threads each run `balance = balance + 100` on a balance of 0. That one line is really three machine steps: read, add, write. Interleave them — both read 0, both add, both write 100 — and the final balance is 100, not 200. One update vanished. Run it again and you may get 200, because timing changed.

**→ The other common shape: check-then-act.** `if (!file.exists()) file.create()` is safe alone and unsafe concurrently — another thread can create the file between your check and your create. The check was true when you made it and false by the time you acted on it.

**→ You don't need threads to have this.** Two browser tabs writing the same record, two servers processing the same queue message, an async callback firing while a request handler is mid-update, two `git push`es to the same branch. Anything with overlapping access to shared mutable state qualifies.

**→ Why it's genuinely nasty:** it's timing-dependent, so it passes tests, passes code review, works on your laptop, and fails once a week in production under load. Adding logging changes the timing and makes it disappear. There is no stack trace pointing at the bug — you just find corrupted data later.

**→ Three ways out, in order of preference:**

**→ 1. Don't share mutable state.** No shared data, no race. Message passing, immutable values, or one owner per piece of data. The only fix that removes the whole class of bug.

**→ 2. Make the operation atomic.** A lock, a mutex, a database transaction with the right isolation level, an atomic compare-and-swap, or a `UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?` optimistic check. The read-modify-write becomes indivisible — nobody can interleave.

**→ 3. Push it to something that already solved it.** A database `UNIQUE` constraint, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, or an atomic counter beats hand-rolled coordination almost every time.

**→ The trap when you reach for locks:** hold them for as little as possible, and always acquire multiple locks in the same order everywhere in the codebase. Two threads grabbing lock A and lock B in opposite orders is a deadlock — both wait forever, and now you've traded corrupt data for a frozen process.
